answer.value: Helion Bio is developing an oral small-molecule therapy for treatment-resistant hypertension. The deck describes a once-daily tablet targeting a renal sodium channel, positioned as an add-on to standard therapy rather than a replacement.
Slide 3 cites the 2025 guideline change lowering the treatment-resistant threshold, which the deck states expands the eligible population by 40%. No source is given for the 40% figure.

The deck states 12 million US patients have treatment-resistant hypertension, that 8 million remain uncontrolled on three or more agents, and that uncontrolled hypertension costs the US system $52B a year (slide 2). None of the three figures carries a citation.

Current care is escalating combinations of diuretics, ACE inhibitors and calcium channel blockers, described on slide 2 as failing in roughly a third of patients. Payors are named as commercial insurers and Medicare; no cost per patient is given.

A once-daily oral tablet inhibiting a renal sodium channel, described on slides 4 and 6. The deck states the mechanism is distinct from existing diuretics because it acts distally, and claims this avoids the potassium loss that limits current agents.

Preclinical only. Slide 7 reports a 22 mmHg systolic reduction in a rat model (n=40) over 14 days, and slide 8 states IND-enabling toxicology is complete. No human data is presented anywhere in the deck.
Dr Amara Osei, founder and CSO, is described as the inventor of the compound with 18 years in renal pharmacology (slide 14). The CEO, Jonas Reeve, is listed as part-time until close of the round.
No clinical development lead and no regulatory lead are named, for a company whose next milestone is an IND filing. The deck names a CRO partner but not a manufacturer.
Slide 9 gives a $9.4B TAM and a $2.1B SAM. The TAM is derived from patient count multiplied by an assumed $2,400 annual price; the SAM derivation is not shown.
Specialty pharmacy distribution at an assumed $2,400 per patient per year (slide 9). The deck models 60% gross margin at scale but does not state COGS.

Slide 11 names two competitors — Vertex Renal and an unnamed Phase 2 asset — and differentiates on the distal mechanism and once-daily dosing. The comparison is asserted rather than shown against published data.
One composition-of-matter application filed in the US and EU (slide 12), stated as pending rather than granted. Expiry is given as 2044. No method-of-use filings are mentioned.
A $1.1M NIH SBIR Phase I award (slide 13), IND-enabling toxicology complete (slide 8), and the patent filing on slide 12. No revenue, no clinical work.
The SBIR award is the only third-party validation in the deck. Slide 15 lists two academic advisors but no customers, partners, or committed investors.
Slide 16 names clinical risk (no human data), regulatory timing, and financing risk, and states mitigations of an experienced CRO and a staged raise.
The deck does not reconcile the 18-month runway on slide 17 with the 26-month timeline to Phase 1 readout on slide 18 — a gap of roughly eight months with no stated bridge.
Raising $6M on a SAFE with a $24M post-money cap and a 20% discount (slide 17). $1.4M is stated as committed. No lead investor is named.
Slide 17 allocates 55% to IND-enabling work and Phase 1, 25% to CMC, and 20% to operations, stating an 18-month runway. The Phase 1 readout on slide 18 sits beyond that runway.
